doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Parents' pride in black artists and education
summary: His parents stressed education and pride in black entertainers, took him to see Ellington, Basie, Ella and others, and he adds thoughts on colleges and big bands.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Your father, and your mother, even though they were into music, still wonder about your choice. Did they have an attitude, pro or con, about jazz in itself?

No, they didn’t have a problem with jazz, because I was very lucky with them, I came from that era of black — there’s that word again — of black families, that stressed a couple of things you and I talked about before. First it was education. They come from that sort of Martin Luther King era where education is your way out, which they imparted that to me and it sticks with me and I still think, and as I study and try to help other people and help myself I realize that by increasing the quality of the product or service that I can deliver to people, I can always hopefully be employed, because the thing I always stress to young people is that you want to be the absolute best at what you do. You can ask any price that way, etcetera, etcetera. So there was the education thing they stressed, which they got from that era, that Martin Luther King era of get out of the ghetto, educate yourself, it goes to the next level. That was the first thing for them. And then the jazz thing, they were from that era of people that were proud of black entertainers. That era of people, it’s so great, they had such pride and like, who was that? Sugar Ray —

The fighter. And even Keter Betts and Houston [Person] were talking about, “Man when he would fight, everyone, it was like that was a rallying point. It was like well they could kick us down but we’ve got the best athletes and we’ve got the best artists. And so we saw, when I was a kid, Leotyne Price, and we were so proud. It was like when we walked © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

into the hall, my mother and father’s head just went a little bit higher. Because they were saying she’s ours. This is something that we’re proud of. And you can oppress us in all these other kinds of ways. But we’ve got these great artists, like Lena Horne they were so proud of, and they took me to see her. They took me to see Sarah Vaughan, Ella Fitzgerald twice, took me to see Duke Ellington three times, Count Basie I went a couple of times, then my father, there was this hall that would always have him, he would just drop me off and eight o’clock and pick me up at about one thirty, five dollars it cost to go in, if you didn’t have a seat, it was a dance. They were so proud of all the great like black artists at that time, and entertainers, like Sammy Davis, who I didn’t get to see, but if these people were on T.V., I don’t know if you remember that group Hines, Hines and Dad, well Maurice Hines, the other Hines brother, he introduced me to my future wife. He became good friends. But whenever guys like that were on T.V., it was like my mom would say, “The Hines boys are on,” or “Lena Horne’s going to be on,” and we’d all run to the T.V. to see this. So my parents didn’t have a stigma about jazz. Their thing was like they were so proud of these people. And they knew that the problem they had was they knew that there were those people who were able to make a good living for themselves, but they didn’t know what these other people did. And that’s why for me they said look, go get an education, get an education degree so you can teach, have something to fall back on, and that’s what musicians do. And so I had that illusion too. So what I had to do and again what I have told students is you’ve got to educate yourself, to find out what musicians do do — oh do, do — that was deep. But find out what musicians do and study them, ask them questions, say what do you do in an average day and how can I get to have — again, with that list, the skills to do those things, how can I prepare myself? And the one thing I know I’m on a tangent, but the one thing I think is that colleges should be doing the same thing because many times I think that unfortunately this whole big band thing that many colleges are into, it’s great and it helps teach ensemble playing, but I want to make sure that when people leave college they’ve got skills to be employable musicians. And a lot of the big band training that they’re getting, I don’t know if that’s necessarily, that should only be a part. Really they could almost start stressing improvisation these days because in the 21st century — my catch word again — I think there’s going to be more opportunities for people to have little niches for themselves. You think of a guy like Anthony Braxton, this guy from ECM Records, he was recording with them for a while, he’s got a market of people that really love his kind of music. And he’s built a little audience for himself. That’s what people are going to be doing.
